--- title: "4. How Hydrophones Work" --- # Overview Hydrophones, derived from the Greek *hydro* (water) and *phone* (voice), are specialized devices designed to *passively* detect acoustic signals underwater. Hence, it is referred to as **passive acoustics**. ::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"} ## Passive acoustics Action of listening to underwater sounds without emitting a signal. This is a non-invasive method to monitor marine wildlife. ::: Several types of hydrophones exist depending on the applications, with different frequency range. Some of the most common applications are: - Marine mammal monitoring, which require high frequency hydrophones - Earthquakes detection, which require low frequency hydrophones - Ambient noise characterization, which require both low and high frequency hydrophones ::: {.fig-full} ![From the whale to the user.](../images/how-hydrophones-work.png) ::: # From pressure to voltage Hydrophones contain a key element, a **piezoelectric** material, which "feels" the pressure change of an incoming sound wave, and converts it into an electric signal. In such, hydrophones are essentially **transducers**, as they simply convert potential energy into electrical energy. ![Conversion of sound signal to electric signal.](../images/hydrophone-signal-schematic.png){lightbox=true} ::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"} ## Piezoelectric Material that generates an electric charge in response to applied mechanical stress. As a wave passes, it compresses the ceramic, which creates a proportional electrical voltage. ::: ::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"} ## Transducer A device that converts energy from one form (acoustic pressure) to another (electrical voltage). ::: The piezoelectric material is often made of ceramics, more specifically Lead-Zirconate-Titanate (PZT) compounds, which are relatively low cost and very effective. It also has high sensitivity and can operate at wide range of temperatures. ![Piezoelectric ceramic plate. Credits: PZT](../images/piezo-ceramic.png){width=60%} # Sensitivity Hydrophones are categorized by their operational frequency bandwidth, which dictates their intended monitoring application: | Category | Frequency Range | Target Applications | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Low-Frequency (Infrasonic)** | $1\text{ Hz} - 1\text{ kHz}$ | Geophysics, earthquakes, large baleen whales (e.g., Blue, Fin) | | **Audio-Frequency** | $10\text{ Hz} - 10\text{ kHz}$ | Commercial shipping noise, fish vocalizations, general soundscape | | **High-Frequency (Ultrasonic)** | $10\text{ Hz} - 200\text{ kHz}$ | Odontocete echolocation (e.g., Orca, Porpoise), acoustic harassment devices | ## Defining Sensitivity Hydrophone sensitivity ($M_\nu$) measures how efficient the transducer converts underwater sound pressure variations into an electrical output signal. Quantitatively, sensitivity is defined as the ratio of output voltage ($V$) to input sound pressure ($p$): $$ M_\nu = \frac{V_{\text{output}}}{p_{\text{input}}} \ \ ; \ \ \text{units:} \left[ \frac{V}{\mu Pa} \right] $$ ## Key factors influencing sensitivity: - **Hydrophone type**: size, design and choice of material (e.g., piezoelectric compound); - **Acoustic frequency**: piezoelectric hydrophones have a resonance frequency which depends on the piezoelectric material. Sensitivity is usually good below the resonance frequency and drops rapidly above. - **Environmental conditions**: water temperature, salinity and pressure can substantially impact hydrophone sensitivity. It is important to calibrate the instrument relative to those conditions. ## Frequency sensitivity curve As demonstrated in the Ocean Sonics high-frequency hydrophone, sensitivity is non-uniform across frequencies. This hydrophone is most efficient at mid-frequencies, and its sensitivity drops below 30 Hz and above 50 kHz. ![Sensitivity curve of an icListenHF high-frequency hydrophone showing empirical HydroCal low-frequency check, Ocean Sonics high-frequency check.](../images/sensitivity-curve.png){lightbox=true} # Signal processing methods Several methods are used to convert the recorded electric signal in data we can analyse. One method is **Fourier Analysis**, where the total signal is decomposed into a set individual frequencies with associated phase and amplitudes. ::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"} ## Fourier analysis Signal decomposition method where a complex signal is expressed as superimposition of simple sine and cosine waves of different frequencies. ::: ![Fourier analysis for signal decomposition. Credit: Medium.](../images/fourier-transform.png){lightbox=true} This way, a time-domain signal is converted into a frequency-domain signal which makes it easier to capture at which frequency most of the energy is. For long periods of sound recording, the signal can be divided into shorter segments of equal lengths, specified by a *time-window*. The result shows how the spectra changes with time, the **spectrogram**. ::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"} ## Spectrogram A visual, three-dimensional representation of a signal's frequency spectrum as it changes over time. ::: ![Example of a spectrogram: time on the x-axis, frequency in Hz on the y-axis, and colour for sound level.](../images/spectrogram.png){lightbox=true} The x-axis is time, the y-axis represents the frequencies in Hz (per second), while the colours represent the level, expressed in logarithm of the signal power in dB. Note on choosing the window: it’s impossible to have a good resolution in time and frequency at the same time (Heisenberg’s uncertainty principle). - Short window = good time resolution, poor frequency resolution - Long window = good frequency resolution, poor time resolution Hydrophones can be put into three categories, infrasonic, ultrasonic, and ?? ## Signal to noise ratio Signal to Noise ratio is an important element to consider for hydrophones. A bigger element increases sensitivity, but also can lower SNR. A rule of thumb is to ensure the measured amplitude is at least 5 times larger than the noise equavalent pressure (NEP) of the hydrophone to maximize the signal to noise ratio (SNR). $$ NEP [Pa] = \frac{\text{Pre-amp Noise} ~[\mu V]}{\text{Sensitivity} ~[nV~Pa^{-1}] \times \text{Pre-amp Gain}} \times 1000 $$ ![Signal-to-noise ratio measures the desired signal against background noise. Credit: Hollyland.](../images/snr.png){lightbox=true} # Other hydrophone types Several transducer designs can record underwater sound. **Ocean Networks Canada uses piezoelectric hydrophones** (Ocean Sonics icListen and GeoSpectrum elements supplied by JASCO). The rest of this handbook refers to piezoelectric hydrophones unless noted otherwise. ::: {.hydrophone-types-table tbl-colwidths="[18,32,50]"} | Type | Operating principle | Notes | |------|---------------------|-------| | **Piezoelectric** | A ceramic element (typically PZT) produces a voltage proportional to acoustic pressure. | Used throughout the ONC network. Sensitive over a wide band; omnidirectional when the element is a cylinder or sphere. | | **Fiber-optic** | Acoustic pressure modulates light travelling in an optical fibre (interferometry). | Immune to electromagnetic interference; used in some long-range or high-EMI applications. Not used at ONC. | | **Accelerometer / inertial** | Measures particle acceleration or velocity rather than pressure. | Useful as a vector sensor for directionality. Not used as ONC's primary hydrophones. | ::: # Passive acoustics applications Passive acoustic monitoring is often associated with underwater soundscapes, but the same instruments support a wider set of ocean applications, from seismology and tsunami detection to marine mammal monitoring and vessel tracking. The table below groups those applications by frequency band. | Category | Applications | Frequency Range |--------|--------|--------| | **Seismic & Geophysics** | Earthquakes, Tsunami detection, Oil & Gas exploration, Seabed mapping, Subsea leakage. | **Sub Hz - 100 Hz** | | **Biological** | Marine mammal vocalization, Ecosystem studies | **10 Hz - ~200 kHz** | | **Natural Ambient** | Ambient noise monitoring. | **10 Hz - 1000 Hz** | | **Naval & Surveillance** | Submarine/Vessel detection, harbour surveillance. | **3 kHz – 300 kHz** | | **Communication** | Submarine communication, navigation. | **3 Hz – 300 kHz** | ::: {#cell-map-output .cell lightbox='true' execution_count=1} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Comparison of frequency ranges across multidisciplinary hydrophone applications.](4-how-hydrophones-work_files/figure-html/map-output-output-1.png){#map-output width=690 height=389} ::: ::: # Resources - Suedel et al., 2019.
